name: Fit-focused dressing for body type (shoulder-to-waist illusion)

angle.text: Users pick garment cuts that emphasise wide shoulders and a narrow waist so the torso reads as a V-taper. The visual change is apparent when the clothes are worn, and the approach is popular in style advice without clothing-specific trials.

summary: Cuts and fit chosen to show off a V-taper; popular in style advice, untested as a clothing intervention.
currentQuick:
This is the practice of choosing clothing cut and fit to emphasise a broad-shoulder, narrow-waist look and downplay other areas.
Body-shape literature links wide shoulders and a narrow waist to perceived attractiveness, but no study has tested whether specific clothing cuts produce that effect.
How it works: Fit and tailoring change where garments sit and how much volume they add, which practitioners say alters the apparent shoulder-to-waist proportion.
Risks and caveats: No health risks are documented for ordinary clothing choices.
deepLead:
Fit-focused dressing refers to choosing garment cuts that emphasise a V-shaped torso, with wide shoulders and a narrower waist, and that minimise features a wearer sees as flaws. The inverted-triangle (V) shape is one of the male body shape categories, described as wider shoulders and chest with a narrow waist.
Wide shoulders and a muscular upper body are linked in the literature to perceived masculinity and attractiveness, and studies cited on Wikipedia found women rate lower waist-to-chest ratios in men as more desirable.
No published trials have tested whether particular cuts of clothing change a man's rated attractiveness.

name: Vertical stripes / monochrome elongation

angle.text: Style advice holds that vertical stripes and single-color outfits make a person look taller and slimmer. The underlying visual illusion has been studied, with mixed results, and the small perception literature points the other way for stripes.

summary: Dressing in vertical stripes or one colour to look taller and slimmer; the small perception literature points the other way for stripes.
note: Published stripe studies report horizontal stripes looking narrower, contrary to the common belief.
currentQuick:
The popular belief is that vertical stripes and head-to-toe single colours make a person look taller and slimmer.
Researchers have tested stripe direction in perception experiments. Two i-Perception studies reported horizontal stripes looking thinner, though the effect varied between viewers. No study on monochrome outfits was found.
How it works: The idea rests on optical illusions such as the vertical-horizontal and Helmholtz illusions, where line direction and filled space alter perceived length and width.
Risks and caveats: No health risks are documented.
deepLead:
Vertical stripes and single-colour outfits are a common piece of style advice, based on the belief that they make a person look taller and slimmer, while horizontal stripes make them look shorter and wider. Researchers have examined the underlying visual illusion, and the results are mixed.
A 2011 study in i-Perception reported that a square of horizontal lines looked taller and narrower than the same square drawn with vertical lines, and titled its finding as horizontal stripes not making people look fatter. A 2013 follow-up reported a similar result for filled squares and found the effect varied between observers.

name: Photo angle maxxing

chain: Camera angle, distance and lens chosen
angle.text: Users test camera angle, subject distance, lens and head tilt to find the framing in which they photograph best. The change in the resulting image is immediately visible, and the lens-distance physics is documented, while attractiveness effects are untested.

summary: Choosing angle, distance, lens and tilt to photograph well; the lens-distance physics is documented, attractiveness effects are untested.
currentQuick:
Photo angle maxxing means working out which camera angle, distance and head tilt produce the most flattering pictures of yourself.
Photography references document that close wide-angle shots enlarge nearby features and longer lenses flatten them. No studies test how such choices affect rated attractiveness.
How it works: Perspective depends mainly on camera-to-subject distance. Shooting from farther away with a longer focal length reduces the relative size difference between near and far facial features.
Risks and caveats: No health risks are documented.
deepLead:
Photo angle maxxing is the practice of finding the camera angle, subject distance, lens and head tilt that make a person look best in photographs. It sits in looksmaxxing communities alongside photography and lighting discussion.
Photography references explain that perspective distortion depends largely on camera distance: close shots with wide-angle lenses enlarge features nearest the lens such as the nose, while longer lenses used from farther away flatten them. Portrait guides commonly cite roughly 75-135 mm (35 mm equivalent) as flattering for head shots.
No studies were found that test whether choosing angles changes how attractive a person is rated, although research on perspective itself is described in photography references.

name: Camera lens distortion (portrait lens 85mm)

chain: Nose and face look more proportionate
angle.text: Users shoot with a longer portrait lens from farther back so features nearest the camera, especially the nose, look less enlarged. The perspective effect is visible in the image itself, and the optics are well documented.

summary: Using a longer lens from farther back to reduce nose and face distortion; the optics are well documented.
currentQuick:
Wide-angle lenses used up close enlarge features nearest the camera, such as the nose. Longer lenses, often cited as 85-135 mm, used from farther away flatten the effect.
The optics are described in photography references. No study has tested how this changes rated attractiveness.
How it works: Perspective is set mainly by camera-to-subject distance. A longer lens lets the photographer stand farther back while still framing the face, reducing relative size differences between facial features.
Risks and caveats: No health risks are documented.
deepLead:
Perspective distortion in photographs makes features nearest the lens look larger. A face photographed close up with a wide-angle lens makes the nose appear bigger relative to the rest of the face, while a telephoto lens used from farther away makes it appear smaller.
Portrait photography references name roughly 85-135 mm (35 mm equivalent) as a good range for portraits, with 75-135 mm cited for head-and-shoulders shots, and note that very short lenses exaggerate the nose and shrink the ears. In looksmaxxing communities, longer focal lengths and greater distance are discussed as ways to reduce this effect in photos.
No clinical or perception studies on this practice were found in the references used.

name: Photo lighting / golden hour

angle.text: Users shoot in golden hour or similarly soft light so faces show lower contrast and gentler shadows. The lighting difference is visible in the photo, and the physics is clear, while the attractiveness payoff has not been tested.

summary: Shooting in soft, low-angle light to flatter your face on camera; physics is clear, the attractiveness payoff is untested.
currentQuick:
Golden hour is the soft, warm light near sunrise and sunset. Photographers favour it for portraits because it lowers contrast and softens shadows.
Whether it makes people look more attractive in photos has not been studied.
How it works: Low sun passes through more atmosphere, so light is warmer and more diffuse, with gentler shadows.[1]
Risks and caveats: No health risks. The only caveat is that effects on perceived attractiveness are unmeasured.
deepLead:
Golden hour is the period shortly after sunrise or before sunset when daylight is redder and softer than at midday. Photographers use it because low sun passes through more atmosphere, lowering contrast and weakening direct light.
Wikipedia says the period is often preferred for portraits when warm, diffuse light is wanted, because shadows are less dark and highlights less likely to blow out. In looksmaxxing and style circles, soft side, window or golden-hour light is described as a way to make a face look better in photographs.
No studies were found testing lighting choice on perceived attractiveness; the Wikipedia article itself does not claim golden hour flatters skin or faces.

name: Dating-profile photo optimization

angle.text: Users pick and order dating-app photos using feedback from tools such as Photofeeler, where anonymous voters rate images. Popular in looksmaxxing circles, it has had little independent testing, and posters note that top-rated photos do not always perform best on apps.

summary: Picking and ordering dating photos with data from strangers' votes; popular idea, little independent testing.
note: Forum reports of rated-best photos underperforming on apps are anecdotal.
currentQuick:
This is the practice of testing dating-app photos, usually with Photofeeler ratings, before choosing which to use. Supporters say it reveals how strangers see a photo.
Evidence is limited: the research comes from the company itself, and forum members report mixed real-world results.
How it works: People upload candidate photos to a rating site, compare scores on attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness, and pick or order photos accordingly.[1]
Risks and caveats: Low physical risk. Reported drawbacks are bias toward certain expressions, discouraging scores, and sharing photos with strangers.[3]
deepLead:
Dating-profile photo optimization is the practice of selecting, editing and ordering photographs for dating apps using feedback or data, rather than personal preference alone. In looksmaxxing communities it is most often associated with Photofeeler, a site where anonymous voters rate photos on attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness.
Proponents say outside ratings reveal how strangers perceive a photo, since friends and family may give overly positive opinions. Forum members also report cases where rated-highest photos did poorly on dating apps, and criticism that raters favour smiling expressions.
No independent studies were found testing whether Photofeeler-optimised photos increase dating-app matches.

name: Photofeeler testing

chain: Scores show how strangers perceive you
angle.text: Users upload photos to Photofeeler to see attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness scores from strangers, and treat it as a looks scoreboard. Its real-world meaning is disputed, with claims that voters favor smiling photos and scores may not match dating-app results.

summary: Crowd-rating of your photos by strangers; popular as a looks scoreboard, with disputed real-world meaning.
note: Scores reflect stranger votes on a photo; independent validation against dating outcomes is lacking.
currentQuick:
Photofeeler is a website where anonymous voters rate photos on traits such as attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness. Looksmaxxing forums use the scores as an informal gauge of looks and of which photo to post.
The company has published its own analyses and a model that mimics averaged votes, but no independent studies were found linking scores to dating results.
How it works: Users upload a photo into a business, social or dating test and receive numerical scores and comments from voters, who earn credits by rating others.[1]
Risks and caveats: Low physical risk. Forum members report scores that feel discouraging or biased toward smiles, and some report results that did not match dating-app performance.[3] Photos are shown to strangers; the site says photos are visible to raters only.[2]
deepLead:
Photofeeler testing is the practice of uploading a photograph to Photofeeler, a website where anonymous voters rate it, in order to see how strangers perceive the person pictured. Photofeeler was founded in 2013 in Boulder, Colorado, by Ben Peterson and Ann Pierce, and offers business, social and dating test types.
In dating tests, voters score a photo on attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness; the other test types use different traits. Users receive numerical scores and anonymous comments, and voters earn or buy credits by rating other people's photos. Looksmaxxing forums use the site as an informal gauge of facial attractiveness and of which photo to use, and members disagree about how well its scores track real-world results.
Published evidence specific to the site consists of the company's own analyses and a 2019 paper by Photofeeler staff describing a neural network trained on its data; no independent clinical studies of Photofeeler testing as a looksmaxxing method were found.

name: Glasses frame selection by face shape

angle.text: Users choose frame shapes to balance or complement their face, for example aiming for a hunter-eyes look. The frames visibly change the face's appearance once worn, and the face-shape pairing rules are widely repeated styling advice without testing.

summary: Choosing frames to balance your face; widely repeated styling idea with no testing behind it.
note: No face-shape rules are supported by published studies.
currentQuick:
This is the idea that certain frame shapes flatter certain face shapes, sometimes pitched as a way to look more angular or add a 'hunter eyes' impression.
No studies were found testing it, and reference sources on glasses discuss lens and frame types rather than face-shape rules.
How it works: Frame lines, colour and size are said to contrast or echo facial features and shift where the eye is drawn.
Risks and caveats: No health risks. Frames that fit poorly can be uncomfortable; effects on appearance are subjective.
deepLead:
Glasses frame selection by face shape is a style practice in which people pick frame shapes intended to balance or complement their face, for example choosing frames to add a perceived 'hunter eyes' look. Wikipedia notes that people often choose frames based on how they look on the wearer.
The Wikipedia article on glasses does not discuss face shape and no studies were found testing whether matching frames to face shape changes perceived attractiveness.

name: Glasses to mask facial flaws

chain: Eye bags, asymmetry or nose less prominent
angle.text: Users wear chunky frames to draw attention away from features they dislike, such as eye bags, asymmetry or the nose. The frames are visibly present and change what stands out on the face, and the technique is a styling trick with no research behind it.

summary: Using chunky frames to hide bags, asymmetry or a nose; a styling trick with no research behind it.
note: Perceived effect is subjective and untested.
currentQuick:
Some people wear thick or oversized frames to take attention away from features they dislike, such as under-eye bags, asymmetry or the nose.
No studies were found testing whether this changes how a face is perceived.
How it works: Frames add visual weight around the eyes and nose bridge, which proponents say redirects the viewer's attention.
Risks and caveats: No health risks. Results depend on the person and are not measured.
deepLead:
Glasses to mask facial flaws is a style practice of wearing thick or large frames to draw attention from features a person dislikes, such as eye bags, asymmetry or the nose. Wikipedia describes glasses as now widely worn as fashion accessories, including non-prescription pairs.
No studies were found testing whether frames conceal or change the perception of facial features.

name: Colored lenses / blue light glasses

angle.text: Users wear blue-light or tinted glasses for screen eye strain and, in some looksmaxxing circles, to reduce puffiness around the eyes. The puffiness link is anecdotal, and the eye-care bodies cited by Wikipedia do not recommend them for strain.

summary: Tinted blue-light lenses sold for eye strain and fresher-looking eyes; eye-care bodies cited by Wikipedia do not recommend them.
note: No studies on eye puffiness; eye-care bodies do not recommend them for general use.
currentQuick:
These are tinted or blue-filtering lenses marketed for screen eye strain and sometimes for less eye puffiness.
The AAO and UK College of Optometrists, as reported by Wikipedia, do not recommend them for general use, and no studies were found on puffiness.
How it works: Coatings or tints absorb part of the blue end of the light spectrum; yellow tints may slightly adjust colour.
Risks and caveats: Low physical risk. Colour distortion can occur with strongly tinted lenses, and benefits are unproven.
deepLead:
Colored lenses and blue-light glasses are spectacles with tinted or filtered lenses marketed to reduce eye strain from screens and, in some looksmaxxing circles, to reduce puffiness around the eyes. By the late 2010s such glasses became popular, with claims ranging from dry eyes and eye strain to sleep disruption and macular degeneration.
Wikipedia reports that the American Academy of Ophthalmology does not recommend special eyewear for computer use and that the UK College of Optometrists says evidence does not support blue-blocking lenses for the general population. No studies were found on tinted lenses reducing eye puffiness.

name: Skin-tone matching foundation / BB cream for men

angle.text: Men use a light foundation or BB cream matched to their skin to even out tone and hide redness and marks. The evening-out is visible while worn, and a well-matched shade is described as hard to detect, though research on male appearance outcomes is limited.

summary: Light base makeup used to even out skin tone; mainstream in cosmetics, with little research on male appearance outcomes.
note: Shade matching varies between brands, and no clinical studies of male use were found.
deepLead:
Skin-tone matching foundation and BB cream are tinted base products applied to the face to even out complexion and cover blemishes. Foundation is a long-established cosmetic category, while BB cream ("blemish balm" or "beauty balm") is a lighter hybrid intended to combine coverage, moisturizer and sun protection in one step.
BB cream was reportedly first formulated in Germany in the 1960s for use on skin after facial procedures, and was developed for daily use by South Korean companies in the 1980s. Western brands launched versions from about 2012, and some critics said these were essentially tinted moisturizers. Some brands, including Korean ones, market BB creams to men.
In looksmaxxing discussion, light base makeup is described as a quick way to even out redness, acne marks or uneven tone. No clinical studies on its effect on perceived male attractiveness were found.

name: Men's makeup (contour, bronzer, highlight)

chain: Darker shade in hollows, lighter on edges
Shadow and light change the face
angle.text: Users apply subtle contour, highlighter and bronzer to make the jaw, cheekbones and nose look more defined. The shading effect is visible while worn and follows standard makeup practice, though male attractiveness has not been studied.

summary: Subtle shading and highlighting aimed at sharpening the jaw and cheekbones; documented in makeup practice but unstudied for male attractiveness.
note: No clinical studies on effects of male contouring on perceived attractiveness were found.
deepLead:
Men's makeup in this context refers to using contour (darker shades), highlighter (lighter shades) and bronzer to emphasize the jaw, cheekbones and nose. Contouring generally uses a shade one or two tones darker than the skin in hollows and along edges to create shadow, while highlighting uses lighter shades on prominent areas.
Contouring has roots in theatrical makeup. Elizabethan stage actors used chalk and soot, and Max Factor Sr. presented a contouring tutorial in 1945. Kevyn Aucoin's 2000 book popularized it, and social media made it mainstream in the 2010s. Male cosmetics were a niche market until the late 1990s.

name: Lip balm / tinted lip color

angle.text: Users apply lip balm, sometimes tinted, to keep lips smooth and add a natural shade. The moisturized, more even look is visible after application, and appearance research specific to lip balm is limited.

summary: Wax-based lip moisturizers, sometimes tinted, used for healthier-looking lips; common and low-risk, with limited appearance research.
note: Some research on lip balms is industry-funded.
deepLead:
Lip balm is a wax-like product that moisturizes and protects dry or chapped lips by forming a barrier layer. Tinted versions add color for a natural lip shade. Common bases include beeswax, candelilla and carnauba wax, lanolin, paraffin and petrolatum, sometimes with sunscreen, flavoring or dyes.
In looksmaxxing discussion, it is mentioned as a cheap way to keep lips smooth and add healthy color. Evidence for appearance benefits beyond hydration is limited.

name: Teeth whitening before photos

angle.text: Users time strips, trays or in-office whitening shortly before a photo shoot or event to brighten their smile. The shade change is visible and measurable on the day, with effects fading over time.

summary: Fast-acting whitening (strips, trays, in-office) timed before photographs; effective short term but with sensitivity and rebound.
note: Part of the effect can fade within days; sensitivity is common.
deepLead:
Teeth whitening before photos refers to using bleaching products or professional treatment shortly before a photo shoot or event to brighten teeth. Methods include dentist-applied peroxide gels, tray-based gels, strips, whitening toothpastes and rinses.
Wikipedia reports that in-office treatment may lighten teeth by 2 to 7 shades, while strips, trays and toothpastes typically produce 1 to 2 shades. Part of the immediate change may reverse within days.

name: Undercut / fade with textured top

angle.text: Users get short faded sides with a longer, styled top, which is widely recommended for many face shapes, and a skin fade is said to make the face and jaw look sharper. The haircut change is immediately visible, and its popularity is documented while attractiveness effects are unstudied.

summary: A short-sided haircut with longer styled top, widely recommended for many face shapes; popularity is documented, attractiveness effects unstudied.
note: Claims of suiting many face shapes come from stylists and forums, not studies.
deepLead:
The undercut is a hairstyle in which the sides and back are shaved or clipped very short while the top is left long, often parted and styled. A fade tapers the sides gradually, and a textured top refers to the longer hair styled with product for volume or a matte finish.
Wikipedia traces the undercut to early 20th-century working-class men, mainstream popularity in the 1920s and 1930s, and a revival in the early 2010s, with adopters including David Beckham. It is frequently cited in men's grooming advice as a default flattering cut; no studies were found testing that claim.

name: Buzz cut for thinning hair

angle.text: Users with thinning or receding hair clip it very short to reduce the contrast between sparse and dense areas. The resulting look is immediately visible, and research on how shaved and bald looks are perceived is mixed.

summary: Clipping hair very short to make thinning or receding hair less noticeable; widely used, with mixed research on how bald and shaved looks are perceived.
note: Does not treat hair loss; it changes how it appears.
deepLead:
A buzz cut is a very short hairstyle, usually clipped to a uniform length across the head. Wikipedia notes it is popular among people with thinning or receding hairlines. "Shaving down" refers to adopting it to reduce the contrast between thinning and denser areas.
Pattern hair loss affects roughly 30 to 50 percent of men by age 50, and is described as moderately stressful and reducing body-image satisfaction. The buzz cut does not treat the condition, which has medical options such as minoxidil and finasteride.

name: Hair length for face shape (long hair maxxing)

chain: Jaw and forehead look more balanced
angle.text: Users match hair length and shape to their face, or grow hair longer under labels such as long hair maxxing, to frame features. The change in outline is visible as the hair grows or is styled, and the idea is popular advice without dedicated trials.

summary: Matching hair length and shape to your face outline; popular style advice with no dedicated trials behind it.
note: Face-shape rules are folk typologies; tight styles are linked to traction alopecia.
currentQuick:
Hair length for face shape is the practice of picking a cut, length or parting meant to complement the outline of the face. "Long hair maxxing" refers to growing hair out to frame or soften features.
Encyclopedic overviews say stylists weigh face and head shape, hair type and the wearer's desired image. No published study has tested whether specific lengths improve rated attractiveness.
How it works: Proponents say length and volume change perceived width and jaw outline through visual framing. This is a styling theory rather than a tested mechanism.
Risks and caveats: Low risk overall. Dermatology guidance links tight braids, extensions and dreadlocks to traction alopecia, and bleaching or dyeing has been linked in some research to health risks.
deepLead:
Choosing hair length to suit the shape of the face, and growing hair longer to frame or soften facial features, is a style practice discussed in appearance-focused communities under labels such as "long hair maxxing". The idea is that length, volume and parting change how the outline of the face, jaw and forehead are perceived.
Encyclopedic sources describe hairstyle choice as depending on several factors, including the wearer's face and head shape from various angles, overall body proportions, natural hair type and growth pattern, and the wearer's desired self-image. No published trial has tested whether a particular hair length improves rated facial attractiveness for a given face shape.

name: Facial hair as camouflage (weak chin)

chain: Beard grown along jaw and chin
angle.text: Users grow a beard to add apparent projection and definition to a recessed chin or weak jawline. The visual change is plain once the beard fills in, and the practice is widespread although no study has tested the camouflage claim itself.

summary: Using a beard to mask a recessed chin; widely practiced, but no study has tested the camouflage claim itself.
note: General beard-perception research exists; chin-specific camouflage is untested.
currentQuick:
This meta is growing or shaping a beard so the lower face looks more projected. It is a common, reversible style choice.
General sources say beards are associated with masculinity and dominance, partly via apparent jaw size, but no trial has tested beards as chin camouflage.
How it works: Facial hair adds visual volume and an edge to the lower face, which proponents say changes perceived chin and jaw projection.
Risks and caveats: Low risk. Beards do not change the underlying bone; surgical options such as genioplasty are separate procedures with their own risks.
deepLead:
Facial hair as camouflage refers to growing a beard to mask a recessed chin or weak jawline. Proponents say beard shape and density add apparent projection and definition to the lower face.
Wikipedia reports that, in evolutionary psychology accounts, beards are said to signal dominance partly by increasing the perceived size of the jaw, and that clean-shaven faces have been rated less dominant than bearded ones, although the origin of beards through attraction versus male competition remains unresolved. No published trial has tested beards specifically as a camouflage for a recessed chin.

name: Posture awareness

angle.text: Users practise noticing and correcting how they stand and sit, countering the head-forward posture of phone and desk use, to look taller and more present. The change in stance is visible while it is held, and posture research has focused on pain rather than attractiveness.

summary: Consciously standing and sitting tall to look more present; posture research is about pain, not attractiveness.
note: Health studies exist; effects on perceived attractiveness are untested.
currentQuick:
Posture awareness means noticing and correcting slouching, rounded shoulders and a forward head. Communities discuss it as a free way to look taller and more confident.
Research mostly covers back and neck pain and ergonomics, with mixed designs. No trial found tests it for attractiveness.
How it works: People use mirrors, photos, reminders or feedback to keep the head over the shoulders and the spine upright. Studies describe photographic and biofeedback approaches for making posture actionable.
Risks and caveats: Low risk. Overcorrecting is not discussed in the sources reviewed; persistent pain is a matter for clinicians.
deepLead:
Posture awareness is the practice of noticing and correcting how one stands and sits, for example keeping the head over the shoulders and the spine upright. In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a way to look taller, more confident and more "present", and to counter the head-forward posture associated with phone and desk use.
Published research on posture awareness mostly concerns health outcomes. A cluster-randomised school trial of a back education programme that included posture awareness training examined back pain and back behaviour in children, and a 2024 study described a photographic method for making posture actionable. No published trial found in this review tests posture awareness for changing perceived attractiveness or presence.

name: Body language / presence training

chain: Open stance, eye contact, slower pace
angle.text: Users train open stance, steady eye contact and slower movement to come across as more confident, often alongside posture and grooming. The research supports increased felt confidence more than measured outcomes in how others judge the person.

summary: Training stance, eye contact and pace to look more confident; the research supports felt confidence more than outcomes.
note: Meanings of gestures vary by culture; power-posing hormone effects were not replicated.
currentQuick:
Body language training means practising open posture, steady eye contact and calmer movement to project confidence.
Power-posing research found reliable effects on how people feel, but not on hormones, and behavioural effects are unclear. Gesture meanings also vary across cultures.
How it works: Practitioners say changing outward behaviour alters how others read confidence and may feed back into mood. Studies support the mood link more than the others.
Risks and caveats: Low risk. Cross-cultural misreading of gestures and eye contact is the main caveat noted in references.
deepLead:
Body language or presence training is the deliberate practice of nonverbal behaviour, such as an open stance, steady eye contact and slower movements, intended to make a person appear more confident or commanding. It is discussed in appearance communities alongside posture and grooming.
Wikipedia defines body language as nonverbal communication through posture, gestures, facial expressions, eye movement, touch and use of space, mostly occurring without conscious awareness. Research on whether trained postures change outcomes is contested: the "power posing" literature found a reliable effect on feelings but no reliable effect on hormones, and an unclear effect on behaviour.
